1.explanation:
• src/language-markdown/parser-markdown.js: This file is responsible for converting the remark AST into Prettier’s internal AST. It currently assigns the entire info string (e.g. "js{cmd=true}") to node.lang. Because remark only splits on the first space, it doesn’t carve out attributes without a space. We need to trim or split node.lang to extract only the language identifier before any attribute braces.

• src/language-markdown/embed.js: This file looks at node.lang to decide whether to embed and format the code block with a sub-parser (e.g. the JS parser). Because node.lang still contains extra braces/attributes, embed.js doesn’t recognize it as a known language and skips embedding. Adjusting embed.js to parse out just the leading language token (up to the first whitespace or brace) ensures that JS blocks with attributes get formatted.
1.bug_scenario: When a fenced code block in Markdown has non-whitespace attributes tucked immediately after the language tag—for example, ```js{cmd=true}``` or ```js {cmd=true}```—Prettier’s Markdown parser fails to recognize “js” as the language. As a result, the JavaScript code inside that block is not handed off to the JS parser/formatter and remains unformatted.

2.explanation:
1) src/language-markdown/parser-markdown.js is responsible for parsing fenced code blocks in Markdown and exposing the `lang` (language) and `meta` (rest of the info string) properties on the AST node. By default it uses remark’s split‐on‐whitespace logic, which doesn’t separate a trailing `{…}` attribute when there’s no intervening space, so `lang` ends up containing the whole string instead of just the language token. 

2) src/language-markdown/embed.js is where Prettier looks at that `lang` property to decide which formatter to invoke. It often does a `.split(/�|\s/)` or similar on the info string, but right now it doesn’t strip off curly‐brace attributes, so it never resolves to the built‐in JavaScript embed function. Both files must be adjusted: the parser to split off attributes into a separate `meta` field even if there’s no space, or the embed logic to strip all non-alphanumeric characters after the first token, so that `js{…}` is treated just like `js`.
2.bug_scenario:
In Markdown files Prettier uses the info string after the opening fence (```) to detect the embedded language (e.g. “js”) and then delegates the contents of that code block to the matching formatter (JavaScript, CSS, etc.). Right now, if you add any extra characters immediately after the language token (for example, attributes in curly braces like ```js{cmd=true} or even ```js {cmd=true}), Prettier will take the entire string (“js{cmd=true}” or “js {cmd=true}”) as the language name, fail to match it against any known formatter, and then drop back to plain‐text formatting. The result is that your JavaScript block with attributes doesn’t get cleaned or line‐wrapped the way a normal ```js block would.

The screenshot in the bug report shows two side‐by‐side previews: on the left you write ```js {cmd=node .line-numbers} and on the right you see that Prettier has not applied JavaScript formatting (it has simply displayed the text unformatted, or shown it as a plain block). The ask is that Prettier should ignore anything beyond the first valid language token ([a-zA-Z0-9_-]) so that attributes don’t prevent correct language detection.
